extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, journalists, and critics interested in news values and news selection
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and evaluate the criteria, assumptions, and values that shape which events and actors become news and how they are reported; includes categories of foreign news, ideological labeling, age/generation framing, and enduring news values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age representation in news
rubrics_metrics.description: People involved in crime or protest are reported as either adolescent or young adult; the majority of news stories are about these age groups. Television news, which appeals to a predominantly older audience, runs comparatively more features about older people than do the newsmagazines, which write more frequently about the young, notably of college-student age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters note age when relevant (e.g., younger leaders replacing older ones). Expect different media to emphasize different age cohorts (TV more older, newsmagazines more college-age). Use examples to show audience-targeting effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generational framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Both news media cluster college students in 'generations' of varying lengths; generations are 'symbolic complexes that typify a period of years and are formed in reaction to major events of that period.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'generation' as a symbolic frame rather than a uniform age cohort; relate generational labels to major historical events (e.g., WWII veterans, 1960s idealists, 1970s silent workers). Use this frame to explain shifts in portrayals of youth over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotyped depictions of young people by class
rubrics_metrics.description: Young people, especially affluent ones, are depicted as violators of adult traditions and restraints; poorer youngsters appear principally as gang members or individual delinquents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to class-based stereotyping in coverage (e.g., Newsweek 1967: hippies, pot smokers for affluent youth; gangs/delinquents for poorer youth). Note how protest participation is framed differently from leisure or delinquency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of ideology in the news
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideology is defined as 'a deliberately thought-out, consistent, integrated, and inflexible set of explicit political values,' and is treated as significant mainly in Communist nations and among adherents of the Left and Right; most American political groups are not treated as ideological under this definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the news' working definition of ideology and how it leads to underrecognition of less systematic value clusters in U.S. politics; analysts should note the consequence that many American positions are framed as pragmatic 'opinion' rather than ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seven-point ideological spectrum and labeling bias
rubrics_metrics.description: The news applies a conventional (seven-position) ideological spectrum from 'radicals' (far left) through 'ultraleft,' 'liberals,' 'moderates,' 'conservatives,' 'ultraconservatives,' to 'right-wing extremists' (far right).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for asymmetries: the 'moderate core' is approved across media; adherents outside the core are treated less favorably. Labels are used unevenly (e.g., 'ultraliberals' or 'left-wingers' used, while 'ultraconservatives' are rarely called 'right-wingers'); radicals and extremists are often conflated with Nazis. Note problems categorizing mixed-position groups (e.g., economically liberal but socially conservative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign news category: American activities in a foreign country
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign stories often focus on what Americans do to, for, and in other countries (presidential visits, diplomats, federal and corporate officials, entertainers, tourists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stories are frequently treated as domestic news; e.g., in Vietnam coverage a high percent of stories were about Americans. Expect more space/time for American actors in foreign contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign news category: foreign activities that affect Americans or American policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries become newsworthy when their activities affect Americans or U.S. interests (Americans imprisoned/killed, harm to American firms, conflicts with U.S. policy) or when foreign happenings mirror or converge with American phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage increases when events have direct American impact or cultural/economic convergence with the U.S.; tourist stories and protection of American landmarks get attention. Crimes are newsworthy when they replicate American crime patterns or violate American mores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign news category: Communist-bloc country activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about the Communist bloc focus on (1) their relationship to the United States and (2) internal problems seen to reduce their power vis-à-vis the U.S.; successes are often labeled 'suspected propaganda' while failures and unrest are emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect interpretation in terms of American strategic interest; personnel changes are read as signs of weakness or implications for U.S. policy rather than routine factional politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign news category: elections and peaceful governmental changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage is limited to elections or appointments of de facto heads of state (ceremonial presidents rarely newsworthy); European royalty is often covered for pomp, while non-European royalty and African dictators receive less respectful treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note selective interest in leadership changes tied to perceived relevance to Americans; symbolic figures may be highlighted for cultural resonance or scorned when perceived as idle/consuming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign news category: political conflict and protest
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign conflicts must be more dramatic and usually more violent than domestic equivalents to break into the news; peaceful demonstrations are rarely covered unless anti-American. Left-wing coups/revolutions often receive more attention than right-wing ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect greater coverage for wars, coups, revolutions, especially when they involve American/Communist allies or have racial/political significance; continuous coverage reserved for high-stakes conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign news category: disasters threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign disasters must be more serious than equivalent American ones to be reported; the farther a country is from America (geographically, politically, culturally, racially), the larger the victim count required for coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Americans among victims or links to U.S. interests as amplifiers; single coverage of famines/tribal wars or repeated coverage depends on perceived relevance to American audiences and cultural similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign news category: the excesses of dictatorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about foreign dictators focus on violations of American political values; dictators are portrayed as having total power and are criticized for brutality or cults of personality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brutal dictators get the most critical attention; non-brutal, conservative dictators may be treated sympathetically, especially if allied with the U.S. Watch for racialized biases in how nonwhite dictators are portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign news: adherence to American values and less detachment
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign news is generally treated with less detachment, and explicit value judgments that would not be considered justifiable in domestic news appear in stories about the rest of the world; foreign news follows American values and often the State Department line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect more overt evaluative language and American-centric interpretations in foreign reporting compared with domestic coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalism as empirical discipline: reality judgments and values
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalism contains findings of empirical inquiry, concepts and methods, and assumptions about external reality ('reality judgments') as well as values or preference statements about how nation and society ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should separate empirical claims, reality judgments, and values; recognize that reality judgments often carry value implications (e.g., assuming the president 'represents the nation').

rubrics_metrics.name: Values are rarely explicit; infer them 'between the lines'
rubrics_metrics.description: Values in the news are rarely explicit and must be found between the lines—in what actors and activities are reported or ignored, and in how they are described (tone, connotations, word choice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts between available neutral terms and chosen loaded terms (e.g., 'turned up' vs 'arrived') as evidence; examine which actors are covered and how to infer implicit values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between topical and enduring values
rubrics_metrics.description: Topical values are opinions about specific actors/activities of the moment; enduring values are preference statements about nation and society that persist across many stories and over long time periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus the analysis on enduring values when seeking long-term patterns; topical values are useful for case studies of particular episodes but do not substitute for enduring-value analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of identifying enduring values (impressionistic/content cues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enduring values were identified impressionistically from continual scrutiny: from actors chosen, descriptions, tones, connotations, and the use of non-neutral terms when neutral ones exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should systematically note lexical choices, recurring story frames, and patterns across outlets/years; examples include differential verbs for similar actions and preferential highlighting of certain violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring value cluster: ethnocentrism
rubrics_metrics.description: American news values its own nation above all; foreign news judges other countries by the extent to which they live up to or imitate American practices and values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for American-centric casualty framing (e.g., counting American killed vs 'Communist death toll'), selective reporting of American atrocities, and framing of regime changes as 'Fall' vs 'liberation.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring value cluster: altruistic democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The news implies that politics should follow a course based on the public interest and public service; it insists politicians be honest, efficient, meritocratic, and dedicated to the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for recurrent news attention to corruption, nepotism, bureaucratic 'waste', and violations of formal democratic norms (civil liberties, due process, integration). Citizen grassroots activity is praised; organized lobbying is treated skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring value cluster: responsible capitalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as one of the enduring values (the news supports certain pro-business norms and expectations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page lists this cluster but does not fully elaborate here; expect coverage that balances praise for enterprise with scrutiny of corporate abuses, and narratives that favor private enterprise with some government intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring value cluster: small-town pastoralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as one of the enduring values (nostalgia for small-town civic norms and the rural town-meeting ideal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for language evoking rural civic virtue, community self-help, and romanticized models of citizen participation as a standard against which national practice is judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring value cluster: individualism
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as one of the enduring values (emphasis on individual initiative and self-reliance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect stories that valorize individual effort, entrepreneurship, and self-help; note tensions when individualism clashes with collective or structural explanations for problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring value cluster: moderatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as one of the enduring values (the news approves the 'moderate core' and pragmatic compromise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage tends to favor centrist, pragmatic actors; political extremes are framed less sympathetically and may be marginalized in news narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring value cluster: social order
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as one of the enduring values (concern for order, stability, and control of deviance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crime, disorder, and threats to public order are frequent news topics; coverage often emphasizes policing, containment, and restoration of order rather than structural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring value cluster: national leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Listed as one of the enduring values (the news endorses certain conceptions of national leadership and holds leaders to public-interest standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders are portrayed as representatives of the nation; stories evaluate their adherence to public service norms, competence, and symbolic role in embodying national ideals.
